title: The Factory Day vs. the AI-Native Day

zones.label: Factory teacher: lecturer and grader
zones.summary: One adult delivers the lesson to the whole room, then grades everyone's work, often late into the evening.
facts: One teacher per room made schooling affordable, but it means one adult must serve every learner's pace (Chapter 3).
A 2022 RAND survey found teachers reported working about 53 hours a week, roughly nine hours more than other working adults. Planning and grading make up much of the difference (Chapter 3).
Gallup's 2022 survey found K-12 workers reported the highest burnout rate of any occupation it studied, with about four in ten feeling burned out always or very often (Chapter 3).
In Mr. Hale's illustrative traditional week, whole-class lecture takes 50 percent of his instructional time, supervising practice 20 percent and grading 15 percent (Chapter 20).
Look for the stacks of ungraded paper, the moon in the window and the lectern waiting by the board.

zones.label: Factory morning: one lesson, one pace
zones.summary: Students grouped by age hear the same lesson at the same pace until the bell rings.
facts: Bell schedule: a typical middle school has six to eight periods of 45 to 55 minutes, announced by a bell (Chapter 3).
Age-based grade levels: Maya is in seventh grade because she is twelve, not because of a test of what she knows (Chapter 3).
Seat time counts hours in the room, not learning. A student who already knows the material and a student who is lost earn the same seat time (Chapter 3).
The Carnegie unit, defined in 1906 as 120 hours of class time in one subject over a school year, still underlies most U.S. high school credits (Chapter 3).
When the bell ends Ms. Rivera's 50-minute lesson on unit rates, half the class has just understood it and the other half is still lost (Chapter 3).

zones.label: Factory afternoon: more of the same
zones.summary: After lunch the same rows, the same pace and the same bell carry on, one subject at a time.
facts: In a traditional school the core academic subjects are spread through the whole day instead of being concentrated in the morning (Chapter 11).
In Chapter 20's 280-student illustration, the traditional afternoon is 10 sections of 28 students, each taught for 240 minutes in the same format.
A standard curriculum gives common content to all, but leaves little room for individual interests or pace (Chapter 3).
In an illustrative fixed 150-hour course, faster students sat through 535 idle hours while six slower students moved on without mastering it (Chapter 3).
To be fair to the model: it educated tens of millions of children and gave every child a seat. Its weakness is that it treats every child in a batch the same way (Chapter 3).

zones.label: AI-native teacher: coach and mentor
zones.summary: The same adults do nearly the opposite work: coaching, mentoring and facilitating instead of lecturing.
facts: Alison King's 1993 phrase sums up the shift: from "sage on the stage" to "guide on the side" (Chapter 20).
In Mr. Hale's illustrative week, lecture and supervised practice fall from 70 percent of his time to 5 percent, and coaching, facilitation and mentoring rise to 70 percent (Chapter 20).
Teacher as mentor is a longer-term relationship, like the advisory teacher who knows a student for years (Chapter 20).
The model does not save on staff. In the 280-student illustration the AI-native day needs about 10 percent more adult-hours, spent on people instead of lectures (Chapter 20).
Risk: some AI-first schools use learning guides who may not be subject experts. Response: make sure a student who needs a human explanation of a hard concept can get one (Chapter 20).
Look for the sticky-note planning board, the dashboard on the tablet and the two chairs facing each other.

zones.label: AI-native morning: compressed and self-paced
zones.summary: A compressed academic morning of about two to three hours, in which each student works at their own pace toward mastery (Chapter 11).
facts: In Chapter 11's illustration the compressed morning is 150 minutes instead of 250, which frees 100 minutes a day, or about 300 hours a year.
Mastery learning: a student shows mastery, typically 80 to 90 percent on a check, before moving on. Each flag on the winding path marks where one student is (Chapter 11).
Gap filling finds and repairs a missing prerequisite, like Maya's fractions, before the student returns to grade-level work (Chapter 11).
Reduced direct instruction: explanation comes in short pieces paced by the student, and the teacher coaches small groups (Chapter 11).

Risk: too much screen time and students working alone. Response: a screen cap such as 120 of the 150 minutes, a break every 25 to 30 minutes, and protected off-screen time with a teacher or classmates (Chapter 12).
The evidence: compression is plausible but unproven, so a school should pilot it and measure the results independently (Chapter 11).

zones.label: AI-native afternoon: pro-social
zones.summary: The freed time goes to people: projects, arts, sports, clubs, making, service and life-skills workshops (Chapter 14).
facts: A pro-social activity needs other people, has a shared goal, has a real audience or real stakes, and ends with a short reflection on how the group worked (Chapter 14).
Chapter 20's illustrative middle school day has 200 minutes of afternoon programming: a project block, arts or sports, clubs or workshops, and reflection.
Chapter 11's illustrative plan for 300 freed hours: 120 for projects with public exhibitions, 60 for arts, 60 for sports and clubs, 40 for life skills and service, and 20 for advisory.

Risk: unstructured drift, like the gym at Lincoln Middle School, where most of about thirty students were on their phones while an adult checked a clipboard. Response: a structured afternoon that is sequenced, active, focused and explicit (the SAFE practices, Chapter 14).
Afternoon groups are smaller than morning sections: a common target is one adult for 15 to 20 students (Chapter 20).

quiz.question: Where does one adult grade stacks of papers late into the night?
quiz.explanation: In the factory model one teacher lectures and grades for every student, and the 2022 RAND survey in Chapter 3 found teachers working about 53 hours a week.

quiz.question: Where would Maya hear the same 50-minute lesson as the rest of her age group until the bell rings?
quiz.explanation: Age-based grade levels and the bell schedule move the whole class through one lesson at one pace (Chapter 3).

quiz.question: Where does counting seat time, the idea behind the Carnegie unit, decide what students have learned?
quiz.explanation: The Carnegie unit counts 120 hours of class time, so time in the seat stands in for learning (Chapter 3).

quiz.question: Where do the same rows and the same bell continue after lunch, one subject at a time?
quiz.explanation: In a traditional school the academic subjects are spread through the whole day (Chapter 11).

quiz.question: Where does a teacher work as a mentor, meeting one student face to face?
quiz.explanation: Teacher as mentor is one of the four roles in the changing teacher role (Chapter 20).

quiz.question: Where does each student move along a learning path at their own pace?
quiz.explanation: The compressed academic morning uses personalized pacing and mastery learning (Chapter 11).

quiz.question: Where would a screen-time cap and a break every 25 to 30 minutes apply?
quiz.explanation: Morning screen-time limits answer the risk of too much screen time in the adaptive morning (Chapter 12).

quiz.question: Where do students build, perform and garden together with an adult who debriefs?
quiz.explanation: The pro-social afternoon fills the freed time with structured work with other people (Chapter 14).

quiz.question: Which part of the day carries the risk the book calls unstructured drift?
quiz.explanation: Freed time that is not planned slides into passive supervision or screens; the SAFE practices are the response (Chapter 14).
